01.note: Four leading Sages, Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva, were traveling together on a ship during the festival of Sukkot, and only Rabban Gamliel had a lulav, which he had bought for a thousand zuz. He used it to fulfill the mitzva and then gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua as a gift. Each Sage in turn used it and gave it to the next as a gift, and Rabbi Akiva, the last, returned it to Rabban Gamliel.
01.why: The mishna rules that on the first day of Sukkot one cannot use another person's lulav; the Gemara cites this voyage to show a lulav given as a full gift works. It also learns from the return that a gift given on condition of return still counts, and from the price how dear mitzvot were to them.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The only one on the ship with a lulav, bought for one thousand zuz; he passes it on as a gift and gets it back at the end.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Receives the lulav from Rabban Gamliel as a gift, uses it, and passes it on.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Receives the lulav from Rabbi Yehoshua, uses it, and gives it to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The last to use the lulav; he returns it to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: The palm branch (taken together with myrtle, willow and a citron) that the Torah commands Jews to take in hand on Sukkot.
The autumn Festival of Booths, a week-long holiday.
A silver coin; a thousand zuz was a very large sum.

02.note: One year the seventh day of Sukkot, the day of the willow branch, fell on Shabbat. Willow branches were brought before Shabbat and left in the Temple courtyard. The Boethusians, who rejected the Sages' view that this mitzva overrides Shabbat, found the branches and hid them under the stones, knowing the Sages would not let the stones be moved on Shabbat. The next day some ignorant people found the branches and pulled them out from under the stones, and the priests brought them and stood them at the sides of the altar.
02.why: Abaye brings this account against Rav Yosef, who held that the willow mitzva consists of standing branches beside the altar. The Gemara reads the ending as showing the willow was taken in hand and waved, and calls it a conclusive refutation of Rav Yosef.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who cites this account to challenge Rav Yosef.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose view about the willow branch Abaye is challenging.

terms.meaning: On Sukkot, willow branches were used in a Temple rite around the altar, with special emphasis on the seventh day.
A Jewish sect of the Temple period that disputed many rulings of the Sages, including this one.
A collection of early teachings from the same period as the mishna, organized like it.

03.note: During the Sukkot water-pouring ceremony at the altar, a Sadducee priest poured the water on his feet instead of on the altar. In anger, all the people pelted him with their etrogim. In the chaos a horn of the altar was damaged that day. They sealed the damaged spot with a fistful of salt, not because this made the altar fit for service, but so the altar would not be seen damaged; an altar missing a horn, a ramp, a base or its square shape is unfit for service.
03.why: The mishna says the priest pouring the water was told to raise his hand; the Gemara brings this incident next to that detail, as the event behind it.

people.name: Sadducee priest
people.about: An unnamed priest who poured the water on his feet rather than on the altar.

terms.meaning: On Sukkot, water was poured on the Temple altar alongside the usual wine offering.
Member of a Temple-era group that rejected many traditions of the Sages, including the water pouring.
The citron fruit carried with the lulav on Sukkot; plural etrogim.
A raised corner piece on each of the altar's four corners.

04.note: Rabbi Yehuda describes the great synagogue of Alexandria in Egypt: a vast basilica with a double colonnade, sometimes holding twice the number who left Egypt, with seventy-one golden chairs. It was so big that a sexton stood on a wooden platform and waved a scarf to signal when the people should answer amen. Craftsmen sat by trade, so a poor newcomer could find his fellow workers and get a living from them. Abaye said all of them were killed by Alexander of Macedonia. The Gemara says it was for settling in Egypt against the Torah's command; when Alexander arrived and found them reading a verse about a nation coming from afar like a swooping vulture, he took it as referring to himself, whose ship had arrived in half the expected time, and slaughtered them.
04.why: The Gemara has just quoted the Sages: whoever has not seen Jerusalem in its glory or Herod's Temple never saw a beautiful city or magnificent building. Rabbi Yehuda's saying about Alexandria is a parallel boast of that kind.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who describes the Alexandria synagogue.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who says all who gathered there were killed by Alexander.

people.name: Alexander of Macedonia
people.about: The conqueror who reads a Torah verse as a sign about himself and slaughters the community.

terms.meaning: The supreme court of seventy-one Sages; the synagogue's seventy-one golden chairs matched its members.
The synagogue attendant.
The response the congregation gives at the end of a blessing.

05.note: Abaye overheard a man telling a woman, Let us rise early and go on the road. Sure they meant to sin, he followed them for three parasangs through a marsh to stop them. They did nothing wrong, and as they parted he heard them say it had been a long way and pleasant company. Abaye said that had it been himself, he could not have held back, and he leaned on a doorpost in regret. An Elder came and taught him: anyone greater than another has a greater evil inclination.
05.why: The Gemara is reading Joel's verses as describing the evil inclination, and Abaye has just said it provokes Torah scholars more than anyone else; this incident illustrates his point.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who follows the couple and then realizes his own weakness.

people.name: a certain Elder
people.about: An unnamed older Sage who comforts Abaye.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
The Sages' term for the inner drive that pushes a person toward wrongdoing.

06.note: Miriam, daughter of a family in the priestly watch of Bilga, abandoned her faith and married a soldier in the army of the Greek kings. When the Greeks entered the Temple sanctuary, she kicked the altar with her sandal and said: Wolf, wolf, how long will you consume the property of the Jewish people while not standing by them when they are in trouble? When the Sages heard of it, they fixed the Bilga watch's ring in place and sealed its niche.
06.why: The mishna says the Bilga watch always divides the shewbread in the south, the side of the outgoing watch, even when arriving; this explains that penalty. The Gemara then asks why a whole watch should suffer for one daughter, and Abaye says a child repeats what she hears at home.

people.name: Miriam, the daughter of Bilga
people.about: Of the Bilga priestly watch; she abandoned her faith, married a Greek soldier, and kicked the altar.

people.name: Greeks
people.about: The army of the Greek kings, who entered the Temple sanctuary.

terms.meaning: One of the rotating groups of priests, each serving in the Temple for a week at a time.
Each watch had a ring for slaughtering its animals and a wall niche for its knives; fixing and sealing them barred Bilga from using its own.
The great altar in the Temple courtyard on which offerings were burned.

07.note: A second account of why the Bilga priestly watch was penalized: once its members were late arriving at the Temple. The watch of Yeshevav, Bilga's brother, came in with those who had arrived and served in the place of the missing members. As a result, Bilga always divides the shewbread in the south, while Yeshevav, his neighbor in the rotation, always divides it in the north. The Gemara remarks that although neighbors of the wicked do not usually profit, Bilga's neighbors did.
07.why: The mishna rules that the Bilga watch always divides the shewbread in the south; this is the alternative explanation to the story of Miriam. The Gemara then notes that on this account, penalizing the whole watch is easy to understand, since the whole watch was late.

people.name: Bilga
people.about: A priestly watch whose members were late to arrive at the Temple.

people.name: Yeshevav
people.about: Bilga's brother, the watch next to it in the rotation, which served in place of Bilga's absent members.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out in the Temple each week and divided among the priests when the watches changed.
One of the rotating groups of priests, each serving in the Temple for a week; the incoming group divided in the north, the outgoing in the south.

08.note: Rav Pappa's host, or by another version a man who came before him, had eggs laid on a Shabbat that fell the day before a Festival, and asked whether he could eat them the next day, on the Festival. Rav Pappa told him to go and come back tomorrow; the Gemara explains that Rav would not give public rulings during Festival days because of drinking. When the man returned, Rav Pappa told him that if he had answered then, he would have forgotten and ruled with Rabbi Yohanan, but Rava had said the law follows Rav in these three issues, whether lenient or strict.
08.why: The Gemara has been discussing eggs laid on a day of rest and the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yohanan about using them the next day; after Rav Adda's answer to his host, this similar case shows that here the law follows Rav.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who is asked about the eggs and delays his answer until the next day.

people.name: Rav
people.about: An earlier Sage whose practice and ruling Rav Pappa follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who disputes Rav; normally the law follows him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who said the law follows Rav in three such cases.

terms.meaning: A biblical holiday on which most work is forbidden, though cooking for that day is allowed.
A speaker who repeated and explained a Sage's teaching aloud to a large audience.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

09.note: Rabbi Eliezer owned a fourth-year vineyard east of Lod near the village of Tavi, close enough to Jerusalem that its fruit had to be brought there rather than redeemed for money. Unable to bring it to the Temple, which had been destroyed, he wanted to declare the fruit ownerless for the poor. His students told him there was no need: his colleagues had already voted and permitted it. The Gemara identifies those colleagues as Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.
09.why: Rav Yosef holds that a ban enacted by a vote needs another vote to lift it, even after its reason is gone. The Gemara points out that the Jerusalem rule ended only because the Sages voted, and applies this to the egg laid on a Festival, whose ban was never lifted.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Owner of the fourth-year vineyard, who wanted to give its fruit to the poor.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The colleague whose vote had already permitted redeeming such fruit.

terms.meaning: Fruit of a vine's fourth year was eaten in Jerusalem, or redeemed for money spent there; farms within a day's walk had to bring the fruit itself.
Fruit formally given up by its owner, which anyone, here the poor, may take.

10.note: A man went around asking, Who has eggs of a live chicken? He was given eggs taken from a slaughtered chicken. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told the sellers it was a mistaken transaction and the sale was cancelled.
10.why: The Gemara explains Rav's statement that an egg is complete only when it emerges: only a laid egg can hatch a chick. Asked what difference that makes, it answers buying and selling, and gives this sale as the example.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who voids the sale.

terms.meaning: A sale based on a basic error about what was sold; it is cancelled entirely, not just adjusted by a refund.

11.note: A man asked the vendors whether anyone had eggs from a hen that had been with a rooster. They gave him eggs that had not been fertilized by a rooster. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told the sellers it was a mistaken transaction and the sale was cancelled.
11.why: The Gemara has explained that only a laid egg can hatch a chick, which matters for buying and selling; this second case of Rabbi Ami's follows the first. The Gemara says the ruling is needed because one might think the buyer only wanted richer eating eggs and was owed just the price difference.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who voids the sale.

terms.meaning: A sale based on a basic error about what was sold; it is cancelled entirely, not just adjusted by a refund.

12.note: Rabbi Hiyya's sons went out to the villages. When they came back, their father asked whether any case needing a legal ruling had come up. They said they had been asked about carrying an attic ladder to a dovecote on a Festival, and had permitted it. Rabbi Hiyya told them: Go out and forbid what you permitted.
12.why: A teaching records Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel arguing over moving a dovecote ladder on a Festival, with Rabbi Yehuda adding that an attic ladder is forbidden to all. The Gemara explains the sons read Rabbi Yehuda as disagreeing with the first teacher, when he was only explaining him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The father, who orders his sons to reverse their ruling.

people.name: the sons of Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: They ruled in the villages that an attic ladder could be carried to a dovecote.

terms.meaning: An ordinary household ladder with many uses, as opposed to one made just for a dovecote; carrying it on a Festival could look like weekday work.
A structure where doves were kept; a ladder was needed to reach the birds.

13.note: By another version, Rabbi Hiyya's sons told him they had been asked about tilting an attic ladder from one window of a dovecote to another on a Festival, and had permitted it. Rabbi Hiyya told them: Go out and forbid what you permitted. The Gemara explains that they thought Rabbi Dosa was more lenient than the first teacher and allowed even an attic ladder, when in fact he was stricter, allowing even a dovecote ladder only to be tilted.
13.why: The Gemara has just explained the first version of this incident; this second version moves the sons' mistake to Rabbi Dosa's ruling in the same teaching about ladders.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The father, who orders his sons to reverse their ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya's sons
people.about: They permitted tilting an attic ladder at a dovecote.

people.name: Rabbi Dosa
people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling on tilting a ladder the sons misread.

terms.meaning: Leaning a ladder from one window to another without carrying it, a lighter act than moving it.
An ordinary household ladder, as opposed to one made just for a dovecote.

14.note: Rav Pappi came to Mar Shmuel's house on a Festival and was served porridge of wheat groats, but he did not eat it, worried the wheat had been pounded that day. The Gemara asks why he did not assume a small mortar and pestle had been used, which is allowed, and answers that he saw it was finely ground. Asked why he did not assume it had been prepared the day before, the Gemara answers that he saw the husks were bright, so it was fresh. Or, the Gemara offers, Mar Shmuel's house was different, since he had slaves, and slaves are lax about such prohibitions.
14.why: Two teachings disagree on whether a small mortar and pestle may be used on a Festival, and Rava said the lenient one is for Babylonia and the strict one for the Land of Israel, where people had servants. This visit tests that distinction in a Babylonian house that had slaves.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: The guest who would not eat the porridge.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The host whose household served it.

terms.meaning: Coarsely crushed grain; pounding grain on a Festival was restricted.
A bowl and club for crushing grain; a large one looks like weekday work.

15.note: Rabbi Eliezer sat lecturing on the laws of the Festival the whole Festival day. As groups left one after another, he called them owners of huge vats, then of barrels, jugs, jars and cups, and when a sixth group began to leave, owners of a curse. When he looked at the students who remained, their faces changed in shame. He told them: My sons, I did not mean you but those who left, who abandon eternal life for temporary life. When the remaining students left at the end, he sent them off with Nehemiah's verse: Go, eat the fat and drink the sweet, and send portions to whoever has nothing, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
15.why: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer could fault the leavers when festival joy is itself a mitzva. It answers that he held festival joy optional: a Festival day should be all eating or all study, while Rabbi Yehoshua said to split it, half for God and half for yourselves.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage lecturing all day, who mocks the groups that leave and comforts the students who stay.

terms.meaning: A biblical holiday, such as Passover or Sukkot, meant for rest and celebration.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

16.note: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel looked sad. Mar Shmuel asked why, and he said he had not prepared a joining of cooked foods before the Festival. Mar Shmuel told him to rely on his. The next year he was sad again for the same reason. This time Mar Shmuel told him he was negligent: everyone else may rely on his joining, but not him.
16.why: The Gemara is asking whether a joining of cooked foods works only if the person it covers knows about it, citing Sages who made one for a whole city. This case shows one man's joining covering others, and its maker refusing to cover someone who was habitually negligent.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose joining of cooked foods covers others, and who refuses it to the blind man the second year.

people.name: the blind person
people.about: He recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel and twice forgot to prepare his own joining.

terms.meaning: Called eiruv tavshilin: food set aside before a Festival that falls on Friday, which allows cooking on the Festival for Shabbat.
Teachings of the mishna, the early collection of Jewish law; some people's job was to recite them from memory.

17.note: Hillel the Elder brought a burnt-offering to the Temple courtyard on a Festival to place his hands on it. Shammai's students surrounded him and asked what animal it was. To avoid a quarrel, he told them it was a female, a peace-offering, and swung its tail so they could not tell, and they left. That day Beit Shammai gained the upper hand and sought to fix the law their way. But Bava ben Buta, an Elder among Shammai's disciples who knew the law followed Beit Hillel, brought all the fine sheep of Kedar in Jerusalem into the courtyard and invited anyone to place hands on them. That day Beit Hillel prevailed, and the law was fixed their way with no one disputing it.
17.why: The Gemara is working through Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's dispute over whether offerings may have hands placed on them on a Festival; this incident shows how Beit Hillel's view became the law.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: Founder of Beit Hillel; he hides the nature of his offering from Shammai's students to avoid a quarrel.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: An Elder among Shammai's disciples who knew the law followed Beit Hillel and brought sheep for everyone to use.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: Founder of Beit Shammai, whose students challenge Hillel.

terms.meaning: Before an offering was slaughtered, the owner pressed his hands on the animal's head.
A burnt-offering, always male, was burned whole on the altar; most of a peace-offering was eaten by its owners.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel, who argue over many laws.
Fine sheep named for a region known for its flocks.

18.note: Some time later, a disciple of Beit Hillel brought his burnt-offering to the Temple courtyard to place his hands on it on a Festival. A disciple of Beit Shammai found him and asked, What is this placing of hands? He answered, What is this silence? meaning that since the law was not fixed their way, the other should keep quiet. He silenced him with this rebuke, and the Beit Shammai disciple left.
18.why: This follows the story of Bava ben Buta, after which the law on placing hands was fixed by Beit Hillel. Abaye learns from the exchange that a scholar who is reproached should not answer back with more than was said to him.

people.name: a disciple of Beit Hillel
people.about: He brings a burnt-offering and places his hands on it on a Festival.

people.name: a disciple of Beit Shammai
people.about: He challenges the placing of hands and is silenced.

terms.meaning: Before an offering was slaughtered, the owner pressed his hands on the animal's head.
An offering burned entirely on the altar.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel, who argue over many laws.

19.note: Rav Avya the Elder asked Rav Huna whether an animal owned half by a gentile and half by a Jew may be slaughtered on a Festival. Rav Huna said it may. Rav Avya asked how that differs from vow-offerings and gift-offerings, which may not be slaughtered on a Festival. Rav Huna said to him: Look, a raven flies. After Rav Avya left, Rav Huna's son Rabba asked his father why he had treated so great a man that way. Rav Huna answered that he was worn out, quoting Song of Songs, and the question needed careful reasoning.
19.why: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai argue over which offerings may be slaughtered on a Festival, and vow- and gift-offerings are forbidden. After this exchange the Gemara gives the answer Rav Huna did not: the gentile's half does not matter, but offerings are eaten at the table of the Most High.

people.name: Rav Avya the Elder
people.about: The Sage who asks Rav Huna the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who answers briefly and then dodges the follow-up.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who asks his father why he treated Rav Avya that way.

terms.meaning: Voluntary offerings brought by choice, not on a fixed day; part goes on the altar and part is eaten by the owner and priests.
A biblical holiday on which most work is forbidden, though slaughtering and cooking food for that day is allowed.

20.note: Shimon the Timnite did not come to the study hall on the night of the Festival. In the morning Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava asked him why. He said a military search unit had come to their town wanting to pillage it, so they slaughtered a calf, fed the soldiers and sent them off in peace. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava said he wondered whether their gain was not outweighed by their loss, since the Torah allows food to be prepared on a Festival only for you, and not for gentiles.
20.why: Rav Huna has ruled that villagers may bake bread for troops on a Festival if a Jewish child could eat some of it; the Gemara brings this incident against him, since the calf could also have been eaten by Jews and yet it was condemned.

people.name: Shimon the Timnite
people.about: He missed the study hall because his town slaughtered a calf on the Festival to feed soldiers.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: The Sage who questions Shimon and condemns what the town did.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.
The Torah's words about Festival cooking, read to mean food for Jews, not for gentiles.
